scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: I don’t have personal opinions or moral judgments, but I can analyze the situation objectively based on ethical principles, communication dynamics, and emotional well-being. Here’s why I’d rate this as **1 (AITA)**—though with nuance: ### **Why it’s *somewhat* AITA (but not entirely):** 1. **Your intent was valid, but the timing/approach may have been sensitive.** - You were advocating for your own emotional well-being (protecting yourself from re-traumatization and fostering a healthy relationship with your half-brother). That’s a reasonable boundary. - However, your mom’s reaction suggests she felt *attacked* rather than heard. She may have interpreted your request as "siding with her ex" or "disrespecting her pain." This is a common emotional trigger in family conflicts, especially when one parent feels blamed for a divorce. 2. **The term "baby mama" is problematic, but not *just* because of your mom’s use of it.** - The phrase is often derogatory, tied to stigma around single motherhood, and can feel dismissive or shaming. That’s why many people object to it. - **But:** Your mom’s use of it might also be a *defense mechanism*—a way to dehumanize someone she resents. Calling her "baby mama" could be her way of saying, *"She’s not a real mother to my husband"* (which, emotionally, she may feel is true). This makes it harder to address without triggering her. 3. **You asked for a *specific change* in *your* presence, not a general apology.** - You didn’t demand she stop talking about her behind her back—just that she respect your feelings by not using that term in front of you. That’s a reasonable boundary. - The issue is that your mom *heard* it as you "defending her," which may not have been your intent. This is where communication styles clash (e.g., your mom might be more direct/emotionally reactive). 4. **The bigger picture: Her stubbornness vs. your needs.** - Your mom’s refusal to acknowledge her role in the divorce (even if she’s sober now) is a long-standing pattern. Asking her to change *one* behavior (the term) might feel like asking her to confront her feelings about the affair/divorce all over again. - You’re right that the name-calling is harmful to *you*, but her resistance suggests this isn’t just about semantics—it’s tied to unresolved grief/anger. --- ### **Why it’s *not* AITA (or why it’s understandable):** 1. **You were protecting your mental health.** - Hearing someone you love (your mom) demean a person you now care about (your half-brother’s mother) is painful. Setting a boundary to avoid that is healthy, not selfish. 2. **You offered a compromise ("just call her 'she'").** - This shows you weren’t demanding she *like* her or change her feelings—just that she respect your emotional space. That’s mature. 3. **Her reaction was disproportionate.** - If she’s truly civil with your dad but still despises his girlfriend, her anger at *you* for asking for respect feels like she’s projecting her own hurt onto you. That’s not your fault. --- ### **What’s the *real* issue here?** This isn’t just about the word "baby mama." It’s about: - **Unresolved family trauma** (affair, divorce, alcoholism, your mom’s refusal to take responsibility). - **Your mom’s need to "win" the narrative** of who’s right/wrong in the past. - **Your half-brother’s presence**—now she has to acknowledge her existence, which may feel like a loss of control. --- ### **What could you do moving forward?** 1. **Reframe the conversation (if you want to try again).** Instead of saying, *"Don’t call her that,"* try: *"Mom, I know you’re still upset about what happened, and I get that. But now that [brother] is part of our family, I need to be able to talk about her without feeling like I’m reliving that time. Can we agree to just call her by her name or ‘she’ when we’re together?"* This shifts the focus to *your* needs (not her guilt) and gives her an "out" (she doesn’t have to like her, just respect your space). 2. **Set a firmer boundary if she continues.** If she keeps using the term, calmly say: *"When you call her that, it brings up hard feelings for me. I’d really appreciate it if we could just use her name or ‘she’ when we’re talking about her."* 3. **Model the behavior you want.** If she’s struggling to call her by her name, you could gently say: *"Her name is [X]. It’s okay to say it—it’s not about approving of her, just being respectful."* 4. **Accept that some things won’t change.** If she’s truly stuck in her resentment, you may need to accept that she’ll never fully respect the relationship you have with your half-brother’s mother. That’s her loss, not yours. --- ### **Final Thought:** You didn’t do anything *wrong* by asking for respect. But her reaction reveals deeper wounds that may take time (or therapy) to heal. The fact that you’re even thinking about this shows you’re a thoughtful, empathetic person—your mom’s struggle is hers to work through, not yours. Would you like help brainstorming how to handle future interactions with her?
